title: Shakuntala
hook: Shakuntala walks into the king's hall with his son, and he says he has never seen her before

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakuntala at the hermitage, saying yes to a king only on a promise spoken aloud. Your line was Shakuntala. Did you say the one thing you needed before saying yes? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-one.

A crowded royal hall, and a woman holding a boy by the hand. No one ever came from the city, so Kanva has sent Shakuntala and her son to the king. She bows and says it plainly: this is your son. Make him your heir, as you promised me at the hermitage. And King Dushyanta looks at her and says he doesn't know her, never married her, has no idea who she is. Everyone is watching. What does she do now?
screen: `I DON'T REMEMBER YOU.` → `THIS IS YOUR SON.` → `EVERYONE IS WATCHING.`

segments.voice: For a moment, the epic says, she can't move. She stands there stunned, ashamed and furious at once, her eyes going red. Then she speaks, and she speaks for a long time. Here is some of what she says, in paraphrase. First, about witnesses. You think you're alone with what you did, she tells him. But the sun and the moon, the wind and fire, the earth and the sky, your own heart, all of them saw. You know, and you're saying you don't. Second, about the boy. A son, she says, is his father born again; look at him and you see yourself, as if in a mirror. Third, when the king answers with insults, about her mother the apsara, and her birth in the forest, she turns his words around. You can see other people's faults when they're as small as a mustard seed, she tells him, and you can't see your own when they're as big as a bilva fruit. Notice what she never does. She never begs. She never pretends the promise was smaller than it was. She stands in front of a king, in his own hall, and tells him the truth about himself. When he still refuses, she turns to go. And then a voice speaks from the sky, telling the king that she speaks the truth, and that the boy is his son. Only then does Dushyanta take them in. Since this is a week's end, look back. The week began with Savitri remembered at a banyan. Then Damayanti, choosing the mortal, searching with a question, naming the wound. And now Shakuntala, in a hall full of people, refusing to be unknown.
screen: `STUNNED, THEN SHE SPEAKS` · `THE SUN AND MOON WERE WITNESSES` · `A MUSTARD SEED AND A BILVA FRUIT` · `A VOICE FROM THE SKY AGREES`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the witnesses. Sit tall, feet on the floor, and let the breath slow. Shakuntala told the king that the sun, the wind, the earth and his own heart had all seen. Feel the floor under your feet. Feel the air on your skin. Notice any light in the room. Let them be quiet witnesses to this moment, to you sitting here. Then turn to your own heart, and let it see you honestly, faults and all, without a verdict. Stay with the breath. If you pray, you can bring it into prayer. The bell holds the time.
Shakuntala. The woman who stood in a king's hall and told him the truth until the sky itself agreed. Today's word.
Your line: Shakuntala. Today, when you spot a fault in someone the size of a mustard seed, look once for one of your own the size of a bilva fruit. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Hindus know Shakuntala's speech at court from the Mahabharata's first book, the Adi Parva; the same story is retold in the poet Kalidasa's later play, which changes how the king comes to forget her.

fork.setup: you're Shakuntala, in the king's hall, holding your son's hand. the king says he has never seen you before. everyone is watching. what do you do?
options: leave quietly, so as not to shame him.
speak, and tell him the truth to his face.
fall at his feet and beg.
fork.reveal: after a moment of stunned silence, she speaks at length: about witnesses, about the son as a mirror, about the faults he can't see. when he still refuses, a voice from the sky confirms her.

original.note: Sanskrit: the epic explains her name from shakunta, bird, for the birds that guarded her as a baby.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shakuntala waited for the king to remember her.
what it means: in the epic, he claims not to know her, and she answers him at length, in his own hall.
what a scholar hears: her speech calls the sun, moon, wind, fire, earth, sky and his own heart as witnesses, and only a voice from the sky ends the standoff.
recall: asks to see her sons once more

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Shakuntala at Dushyanta's court; his denial; her speech: the witnesses, the son as the father's self, the mustard seed and the bilva fruit; the king's insults; the voice from the sky)
